newsitem.title: FRANCE: New wrangle as Elf refinery strike enters week two.
newsitem.headline: New wrangle as Elf refinery strike enters week two.

text.p: A French refinery strike at Elf Aquitaine entered its second week on Thursday amid new wrangling over Elf's plans to cut jobs but lingering uncertainty over union efforts to widen the protest to other oil firms.

Talks are set for 1300 GMT on pay and working conditions which Elf says it is willing to negotiate. But union officials reiterated they would demand discussion of job cut plans which sparked the strike at Elf's three French plants a week ago.
Some workers also quarrelled with a deal between unions and bosses to allow brief oil product deliveries out of storage at the stricken refineries once talks got underway in Paris.
The agreement would let certain products out of the Donges, Feyzin and Grandpuits plants for a day in return for the talks, but some grassroots employees disapproved, union officials said.

"Some of our guys are saying it will just give the company a chance to fill up its depots again or get everything out by tanker," said a union official at Donges in western France, France's largest refinery.
Word had gone round that Elf had chartered four tankers and they were headed for the coastal refinery, he said.
Elf had no immediate comment on this.

The strike over 330 job cuts at Elf's Antar subsidiary has frozen its French refining output and three quarters of its European capacity, causing a logistical knot and helping to drive up international gasoline prices.
Officials at other oil companies said they were meanwhile waiting for confirmation and further details of union plans to call a nationwide oil strike for December 10.
Labour leaders proposed the action after talks between five main French unions on Wednesday, saying part of the plan was already afoot and a national strike would complete the picture.

Both oil company and union officials said there clearly was a risk of disruption over the next week -- including a possible one-day strike called at Shell's Berre refinery -- but there was little sign of national momentum growing yet.
"It's too early to say, but we obviously hope this is going to happen," said one union official.
Unions are protesting about cost-cutting in the refining sector which they say threatens 1,700 jobs. Oil companies say there is a glut of spare capacity and savings are inevitable.
Union officials said workers at the Trapil pipeline company linking many oil facilities had meanwhile started their own disruption, but there was no immediate confirmation.
